books.section: Topic 4.11 An Age of Reform, B. Debating the Future of Slavery in America

primary_sources: Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, 1845

stimulus.text: "The more I read, the more I was led to abhor and detest my enslavers. I could regard them in no other light than a band of successful robbers, who had left their homes, and gone to Africa, and stolen us from our homes, and in a strange land reduced us to slavery." — Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, 1845
stimulus.source_note: Verbatim public-domain quotation from Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass (Boston: Anti-Slavery Office, 1845), Chapter VII. Wording checked against the Project Gutenberg text and the UNC Documenting the American South edition.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain quotation from Douglass, Narrative (1845)
stem: According to Douglass, learning to read led him to

options.text: accept slavery as a natural and unchangeable condition
options.misconception: Reading made Douglass hate slavery more, not accept it.

options.text: forgive his enslavers for their cruelty toward him
options.misconception: Douglass calls them robbers and loathes them; forgiveness is nowhere in the passage.

options.text: see his enslavers as robbers and hate slavery more
forget the African home he had been stolen from
options.misconception: Douglass remembers the theft from Africa; reading sharpened the memory, not erased it.

rationales.A: Douglass says reading brought 'another even more painful' difficulty. It deepened his hatred of slavery, not his acceptance of it.
rationales.B: Douglass says he loathed his enslavers as the meanest and most wicked of men. That is the opposite of forgiveness.
rationales.C: Douglass writes that the more he read, the more he was led to abhor his enslavers, seeing them as robbers who stole his people from Africa.
rationales.D: Douglass remembers the stealing from Africa in detail. Reading gave him words for the crime; it did not make him forget it.
rationales.general:
1. Follow the chain. Reading gave Douglass words to meet the arguments for slavery.
2. Watch the cost. The same reading made him abhor his enslavers more, not less.
3. Name the result. Knowledge turned a slave's suffering into a clear charge: robbery.
Background: Douglass learned to read in Baltimore, where his enslaver warned that learning would unfit a slave for slavery.
Remember: in a slave narrative, reading is never neutral — ask what the reader does with it.
